memory_leads.lead: Sale-and-purchase brokers form a vessel-asset matching and information layer between sellers and buyers, circulating opportunities, indications and bids while often helping translate market intelligence into transaction momentum; the category matters without ranking broker houses.

Vessel marketing can move from confidential/off-market approaches through circulars or broader broker distribution to indications, offers and counters; sale liquidity is therefore partly an information-distribution process rather than an exchange-traded market.

Buyer technical inspection and documentary due diligence connect physical condition, machinery/records, class status, survey history and expected capex to bid value; an operational vessel can still carry transaction-specific technical uncertainty.

Ship valuation commonly draws on recent comparable sales, vessel age/specification, builder/yard reputation, class/survey position, earnings expectations, replacement/newbuilding cost and market liquidity; the useful memory category is multi-input asset valuation, not exact price estimates.

A memorandum-of-agreement style sale contract converts negotiated commercial terms into a closing process with deposit, documentary obligations, conditions, notices and delivery mechanics; exact standard forms and clause effects are deferred.
Deposits and escrow or stakeholder arrangements can bridge signing and closing, creating a separate custody/default-risk stage before the remaining purchase price changes hands.
Financing or corporate approvals and other transaction conditions can leave a signed or agreed sale exposed to closing risk; commercial agreement and completed ownership transfer are distinct states.

An encumbered vessel sale requires coordination with lenders or secured parties so mortgages or other security can be released/discharged against payment; P015 financing state therefore enters the closing critical path.

Documentary closing can include bill-of-sale/title instruments, corporate authority, registry/deletion documents and other certificates; the structural point is that legal/documentary title readiness must align with payment and physical delivery.

Physical delivery is a timed operational cutover at an agreed place/window with condition and readiness implications; ownership economics can shift at a specific delivery state rather than at negotiation or signing.

Remaining bunkers, lubricants, stores or other onboard inventories can be measured and settled separately at delivery, linking P005 measurement concepts to vessel transfer without changing the headline ship price.

Flag/registry deletion and new registration, and potentially class continuity or transfer, create administrative cutovers around delivery; an ownership transfer can be commercially agreed before every post-delivery operating credential is ready.

A vessel may be sold charter-free or with employment/charter interests that require assignment, novation or agreed continuation; attached cash flows and redelivery timing can materially alter transaction structure and value.

Survey/drydock position and near-term capex refine the atlas asset-price cycle: two similar-age ships can have different economic value because the buyer inherits different maintenance and compliance timing.

Distressed sales, lender-driven disposals and opportunistic acquisitions refine the capital-cycle memory by showing that the same asset-price trough can transfer vessels from leveraged sellers to buyers with stronger liquidity rather than simply remove capacity.

Sale for continued trading is structurally distinct from P006 sale-for-recycling: both transfer title, but the buyer's operating, class/flag and delivery requirements differ from an end-of-life final-voyage chain.

Crew, management, insurance and operational responsibility can change at or around delivery, so the transaction should be replayed as a coordinated control handover rather than only a registry ownership event.
The broad statement that freight-rate and asset-price changes generate outsized owner balance-sheet effects is already covered by the atlas asset operating leverage and capital-cycle leads.
Class, flag and survey status as commercial-operability constraints are already established in P011/P015; P016 retains only their role in transaction valuation and cutover.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory cannot support exact transaction prices, valuation marks, premiums/discounts or current broker assessments; these require dated source-first Evidence.
MOA vocabulary is useful orientation but exact form versions, conditions, remedies, deposit/default and governing-law effects require Evidence.
No reliable basis for exhaustive historical rankings or company lineages; such enumeration would introduce salience and geography bias.
Document, notarization, registry, tax and title requirements differ across flags/jurisdictions and periods and are deferred.

stop_reason: The trading-vessel S&P chain is populated from marketing through valuation, inspection, financing release, documentary closing and physical delivery; further blind recall becomes transaction-, broker-, form-, price-, flag- or jurisdiction-specific.

method_observation.observation: A ship sale is best replayed as synchronized changes in price/payment, debt/security, title, physical possession, charter employment, class/flag/registry and operating control; treating the sale date as one atomic fact hides closing risk and economic timing.

truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no sale price, valuation, contract term, title/security effect, registry rule, closing result or historical transaction fact is verified.
